papers.title: Learned Warm Starts for Steady Transonic RANS Simulations of Wing and Aircraft Configurations
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates can accelerate many-query aerodynamic analyses, but their standalone predictions may be insufficiently accurate or robust to support reliable design evaluations. We develop a learned warm-start formulation that predicts mean-flow and turbulence fields directly on native CFD meshes for subsequent correction by the RANS solver. A common architecture and objective structure are used across subcritical and transonic flows, including challenging conditions with shock-induced separation. A condition-modulated Transolver combines Fourier and wall features with target-gated regularization, a Sobolev-type loss, adaptive loss weighting and sampled training. Prediction requires no preliminary flow solution, and training requires no solver-residual evaluation. Extensive 3D CFD evaluations on SuperWing, the NASA Common Research Model (CRM) and DLR-F6 assess geometric and operating-condition generalization, including interpolation, extrapolation and cross-mesh deployment, using Spalart-Allmaras and $k$-$\omega$ SST closures on million-cell meshes. Unseen nominal cases achieve geometric-mean iteration speed-ups of approximately $2$-$4\times$ under a common convergence criterion based on cold-run aerodynamic coefficients. On CRM, learned initialization provides greater aggregate acceleration than nearest-condition restarts using the same solution library. Resolution invariance enables direct deployment of coarse-mesh models on finer meshes without retraining, solution interpolation or target-condition coarse solves. Including data generation and training, estimated campaign speed-ups reach $2.1$-$2.3\times$. No warm run diverges; fewer than $2\%$ fail to satisfy the cold-reference convergence criterion. These results support learned initialization for repeated aerodynamic analyses, while highlighting initialization sensitivity near separation as a remaining limitation.

papers.title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

papers.title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
papers.abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.

papers.title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH
papers.abstract: Accurate computation of the acoustic terms in weakly-compressible SPH, including the equation of state, its inverse, and the evaluation of the local speed of sound, is essential to ensure energy conservation, robust solid boundary conditions, and correct open boundary behavior. In the classic Cole's equation of state, using values of the polytropic constant $\gamma \ne 1$ can lead to significant precision loss, particularly when computations are performed in single precision, as is common in GPU implementations. We extend here our previous results on the optimal choice of state variable by introducing a new higher-precision form for all three acoustic terms, denoted \texttt{explog}, and assess its numerical accuracy and computational performance across a variety of devices and test cases. We find that the new form evaluates the acoustic terms with a maximum ULP of~2 for arguments less than $0.125$, and has higher errors in less than 1\% of the arguments larger than the threshold. Combined with a rewritten expression of the pressure at solid boundary particles in the ``dummy'' model, it provides consistently more accurate results, maintaining deviations from the reference pressure profile to below 2\%, even in presence of a rough bottom terrain. Computationally, the new formulation is also faster than the naive one on GPU, and only marginally slower on CPU.

papers.title: OPINE: Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings for Turbulent Flows
papers.abstract: Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) represents physical fields with orthogonal modes ordered by variance, so that one decomposition gives reduced coordinates in every dimension, but it needs many modes when the data lie near a curved manifold. Nonlinear autoencoders are more compact, but their information loss happens inside a nonlinear encoder, and a model trained with one latent dimension gives no model with a smaller one. We introduce Orthogonal Projection in Invertible Nonlinear Embeddings (OPINE), which learns an invertible nonlinear change of coordinates and performs POD in the transformed coordinates. Because the map is invertible, all information loss occurs in the POD projection, and ordering its basis after training gives reduced coordinates of every smaller dimension from a single model. Training alternates gradient updates of the map with a damped update that tracks the evolving POD subspace, and we prove that this update converges locally to the exact POD subspace. We evaluate OPINE on synthetic manifolds, chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics, forced Burgers turbulence, two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow, and three-dimensional minimal channel flow. OPINE is more accurate than POD at every tested retained dimension above one, and on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Burgers dynamics, it is more accurate than convolutional and fully connected autoencoders by more than two orders of magnitude at the largest retained dimension.

papers.title: Variational learning of energy-stable macroscopic flow equations from microscopic laws
papers.abstract: We present a generalized variational approach for constructing energy-stable macroscopic partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from microscopic physical laws. Rather than fitting the PDE evolution for prescribed variables from macroscopic trajectories, we construct an extendable variational structure by adjoining auxiliary variables to seek autonomous reduced dynamics in an enlarged state space. By defining these variables as micro--macro encoders with explicit microscopic counterparts, we cast the learning problem as the sample-wise joint identification of the reduced state representation and the variational ingredients from time-discrete data, enabling systematic law-level transfer across scales. The resulting PDEs preserve frame indifference, physical constraints, and energy stability by construction, and admit a fluctuation--dissipation-consistent stochastic extension. Numerical results for the non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric fluids show that the learned models capture the viscoelastic responses induced by nonlinear and heterogeneous molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.

papers.title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
papers.abstract: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$\omega$-$\gamma$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

papers.title: Predicting Time-Dependent Flow Over Complex Geometries Using Operator Networks
papers.abstract: Developing neural surrogates for unsteady flow that generalize across complex geometries and maintain accuracy over extended rollouts remains a critical challenge for accelerating flow simulations. We present a time-dependent, geometry-aware Deep Operator Network that predicts velocity fields for moderate-Re flows around parametric and non-parametric shapes. The model encodes geometry via a signed distance field (SDF) trunk and flow history via a CNN branch, and is trained using 841 high-fidelity simulations from the FlowBench dataset (https://baskargroup.bitbucket.io/). The model attains $\sim 5\%$ relative L2 single-step error and up to 1000x speedups over CFD on 262 test geometries not used for training. We provide physics-centric rollout diagnostics, including probe-based phase lag and Strouhal frequency analysis, to quantify long-horizon fidelity. These reveal accurate near-term transients but systematic error accumulation in fine-scale wakes, most pronounced for sharp-cornered geometries. We analyze failure modes and outline practical mitigation strategies including physics-informed regularization and diffusion-based refinement. Code, splits, and scripts are openly released at: https://github.com/baskargroup/TimeDependent-DeepONet to support reproducibility and benchmarking.

papers.title: A unifying view of averaging for wave-mean flow decomposition
papers.abstract: Geophysical flows are routinely decomposed into mean flow and waves, and the procedure used determines how the motion is divided between the two. Ideally, the wave and mean motions of interest evolve on distinct timescales, in which case they can be separated by taking an infinite-time average over all wave periods. Individual waves average away, while exactly resonant interactions contribute to the averaged dynamics because they are steady on the fast timescale. We generalize this averaging to finite windows, yielding a family of decompositions that additionally retain near-resonant interactions whose phases do not fully cancel over the time window. Such averaging necessarily invokes a choice of reference frame; the same flow averaged in two frames may yield mean flows differing by a drift. The averaging formulation developed here enables us to express Stokes drift through resonant and near-resonant interactions, confirming the intuition that it is a slow quantity generated by fast waves and revealing a coherent near-resonant contribution generally present in Stokes drift calculated over finite time from broadband wave fields. We use the fast-wave evolution underlying the exact average to define both the wave reference frame, in which the fast phase is steady, and a wave-frame average. We cast familiar Eulerian and Lagrangian averages and this wave-frame average in a common form to further illustrate how the chosen frame determines which motions enter the mean. This view of averaging provides a common basis for comparing decompositions and choosing among them according to the physical processes one seeks to isolate.

papers.title: Enriched Surface Thermodynamics for Sharp-Interface Fluid Models
papers.abstract: A sharp interface can retain material and structural information about an unresolved fluid transition zone. We formulate a local thermodynamic framework for isotropic surfaces carrying constituent surface mass densities and a thickness descriptor. The distinction between densities of additive contents and internal descriptors determines the area conjugate, reversible surface stress, and Gibbs-Duhem relation. A volume-per-area thickness has a pressure-like conjugate, a mechanical work contribution, and a separate evolution equation. Independent, constrained, and rapidly equilibrating thicknesses require different kinematics and reductions. Material storage can be retained without retaining surface inertia. The balances and entropy production specify admissible exchange and structural relaxation. For a moving surface patch, an available-free-energy identity accounts for mechanical power and for the contributions of material and structural fluxes across its boundary. Equilibrium reduction retains the production and transport needed to follow the reduced state. An explicit mass-thickness free energy has a positive-definite material Hessian and gives coupled adsorption, expansion, compression, and dissipative relaxation. Pressure response yields conditional restrictions on reduced states and demonstrates that distinct independent and constrained states can share an entire pressure-tension curve. Geometric thickness realizations and finite-rate transfer are treated with their associated mechanical and balance requirements. The framework separates state selection, constitutive closure, reduction, and identification from observations.

papers.title: Residual correction for accelerating dual-time-stepping lattice Boltzmann methods
papers.abstract: For lattice Boltzmann simulations of unsteady flows at low Reynolds numbers, dual-time stepping decouples the physical time step from lattice streaming, yet conserved-moment iteration errors decay slowly at large steps. We develop a residual correction method based on the conserved-moment structure of the collision operator. With fixed step histories and both relaxation rates equal to unity, post-collision populations depend on incoming populations only through reconstructed conserved moments, so one collision eliminates local perturbations with zero conserved moments. Periodic rest-state linearization shows that, at large physical steps, the contraction factor of the uniform conserved mode approaches unity, while its moment residual scales inversely with the step relative to macroscopic error. On periodic domains, combining this scaling with linearized acoustic propagation and viscous diffusion yields a macroscopic auxiliary system driven by the conserved-moment residual and solved in Fourier space for low-wavenumber errors. For solid walls, reference-state linearization of the complete sweep, including executed bounce-back updates, yields a sparse kinetic correction. Both auxiliary systems compute increments from the full nonlinear residual, and we prove fixed-point equivalence with the original discrete system, preserving unsteady and nonlinear convective effects. Refining the time step on fixed grids verifies second-order temporal self-convergence of slowly varying periodic velocity fields in two and three dimensions. Under fixed physical steps and tolerances, mean inner sweeps per step drop from hundreds in three-dimensional periodic flow and thousands in a two-dimensional cavity to a few.

papers.title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
papers.abstract: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}\rho U^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.

papers.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
authors: Christopher L. Wirth (Case Western Reserve University)
papers.abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

papers.title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure
papers.abstract: Moisture transport in cement-based materials involves transient multiphase flow through highly irregular pore networks, where evolving air--water interfaces strongly influence liquid invasion and gas displacement. Here, pore-resolved, image-based direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate spontaneous imbibition in a FIB--SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure, resolving air--water interface dynamics at nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales and nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As these dynamics remain inaccessible to direct experimental observation at such scales, the simulations provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first direct view of transient imbibition within the capillary porosity of a realistic cementitious microstructure. The three-dimensional simulations reveal highly heterogeneous wetting-front propagation, continuous interface reconfiguration, and progressive air entrapment, showing that local dynamics depend on evolving interface curvature and capillary-pressure fields rather than on characteristic pore size alone. Significant air entrapment develops even within the capillary pores and under perfectly water-wetting conditions, progressively reducing the saturation rate, while the capillary pressure of trapped-air clusters depends strongly on local interface geometry rather than gas volume alone. Controlled two-dimensional analyses show that the balance between capillary, viscous, inertial, and gravitational effects is strongly scale-dependent. Comparison with the three-dimensional simulations highlights the importance of out-of-plane interface curvature and pore-network connectivity. The framework also resolves moisture conditions at the steel--concrete interface, illustrating its potential for corrosion-relevant pore-scale analysis.

papers.title: Jovian Polar Vortex Generation in a Shallow-Water Model with Quasi-Stochastic Convection
papers.abstract: The mechanisms governing the formation and maintenance of polar vortices on Saturn and Jupiter represent a significant challenge in current planetary atmospheric dynamics. In the presence of internal heat sources, the existence of condensable components leads to widespread moist convection in the polar regions of these gas giants. However, the role of moist convective organization in the formation and maintenance of such polar vortices remains poorly understood. To investigate the interaction between convection and polar vortices, this study develops a polar $\gamma$-plane shallow-water model coupled with a quasi-stochastic convective parameterization. In this quasi-stochastic scheme, convection is prescribed as localized impulsive mass sinks, with the inception probability depending on local vorticity, thereby assigning a higher convective likelihood to cyclonic regions. Numerical experiments successfully reproduce shielded cyclones and persistent vortex crystals reminiscent of Jupiter's polar configuration. Increasing mesoscale feedback promotes vortex growth, shield formation, and spectral organization, while the characteristic vortex scale depends on both the deformation radius and the convective parameterization. The resulting patterns exhibit both clockwise and counterclockwise structural drift, whose direction and rate are not adequately captured by a conventional Rossby wave phase-speed estimate. A Biot--Savart diagnostic reveals competing contributions to structural drift, with predominantly counterclockwise advection induced by the other vortices and clockwise advection induced by the background vorticity outside the identified vortices. These results provide a possible formation pathway for shielded vortex crystals and highlight the role of convective feedback in vortex formation.

papers.title: Internal heating in rapidly rotating convection is not a shortcut to geostrophic turbulence
papers.abstract: Convective turbulence in planets and stars is often driven by internal heating. This forcing mechanism has also been proposed as a means of accessing the diffusion-free scalings of the geostrophic turbulence (GT) regime at modest forcing. We test this with the asymptotically reduced quasi-geostrophic model, which is formally valid in the limit of vanishing Ekman number, $Ek \rightarrow 0$, and retains the Prandtl number as an independent parameter. We find no such shortcut: the Nusselt and Reynolds numbers are no closer to their diffusion-free predictions than in the boundary-heated case; the predicted $Pr^{-1/2}$ collapse fails over the range surveyed; and the prefactor depends on the form of the heating. Our no-slip/stress-free cases track the radiatively driven simulations of Hadjerci, Bouillaut, Miquel & Gallet (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 998, 2024, A9) case by case. Those simulations span only the narrow range of forcing over which the compensated Nusselt number is near its maximum within their geostrophic-turbulence criterion; across the wider range accessible to the reduced model it rises to that maximum and then falls by more than an order of magnitude while the flow remains rotationally constrained. We argue that bulk transport scalings are incomplete diagnostics of GT, whereas the saturation of the interior mean temperature gradient and of the vertical velocity kurtosis remain reliable indicators.

papers.title: Ewald summation of doubly periodic 2- and 3-dimensional Stokes multipoles
papers.abstract: In spite of the qualitative differences between Stokes flows in 2 and 3 dimensions, most particle-resolved computational studies of microswimmers and other colloidal systems dominated by low-Re hydrodynamic interactions are carried out in triply periodic geometries, while the corresponding continuum descriptions are frequently solved in 2-dimensional doubly periodic domains. Furthermore, most experimental examples of biological and synthetic microswimmers are realised in confined, quasi-2-dimensional geometries with a finite thickness in one of the three dimensions. To enable studying the non-trivial differences between these system geometries, in this paper we systematically derive Ewald representations for periodic Stokes force multipoles in geometries with two periodic directions, treating both three-dimensional Stokes flow with one unbounded coordinate and intrinsically two-dimensional singularities. Starting from the periodic Stokeslet, we obtain explicit expressions for force dipoles and quadrupoles and analyse the non-trivial zero-wavevector contribution arising under partial periodicity. The analytical expressions are independently validated by comparing with results from an explicit lattice Boltzmann solver in each geometry.

papers.title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
papers.abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

papers.title: Dynamics of a two-dimensional microswimmer near a slippery boundary
papers.abstract: Microswimmers near walls and interfaces can switch between qualitatively different modes of motion depending on the slip properties of the neighbouring boundaries. To study this theoretically, a two-dimensional point-singularity model of a microswimmer, which does not self-propel in unbounded fluid, is placed near a flat viscosity discontinuity between two fluids with viscosity ratio $\sigma$, and also near a partial-slip wall with Navier-slip length $\lambda$. Using complex-variable methods, the dynamical systems governing the swimmer motion are derived explicitly in both scenarios. Near the viscosity discontinuity, below a universal critical viscosity ratio $\sigma_c=1/2$, the swimmer is trapped at a fixed height with its stresslet axis normal to the boundary. When $\sigma=\sigma_c$ it glides parallel to the boundary at a speed selected by its orientation, with a terminal speed determined by its initial state. For $\sigma>\sigma_c$ it oscillates periodically in height and orientation while drifting along the boundary. The dynamics near a partial-slip wall depend on the ratio of the slip length to the length scale of the singularity and are similar in exhibiting an analogous transition at a critical slip length. It is found, however, that the dynamics near a viscosity discontinuity for $\sigma$ above $\sigma_c$ are richer than those near the partial-slip boundary, including the existence of a hydrodynamic bound state with zero net displacement over one period. Although the study is limited to two dimensions, these results show how a single boundary parameter organises qualitatively distinct modes of locomotion, in close analogy with slip-induced transitions reported for three-dimensional swimmers.

papers.title: Achieving angular-momentum conservation with physics-informed neural networks in computational relativistic spin hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: We propose physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a numerical solver for relativistic spin hydrodynamics and demonstrate that the total angular momentum, i.e., the sum of orbital and spin angular momentum, is accurately conserved throughout the fluid evolution by imposing the conservation law directly in the loss function as a training target. This enables controlled numerical studies of the mutual conversion between spin and orbital angular momentum, a central feature of relativistic spin hydrodynamics driven by the rotational viscous effect. We present two physical scenarios with a rotating fluid confined in a cylindrical container: one case in which initial orbital angular momentum is converted into spin angular momentum in analogy with the Barnett effect, and the opposite case in which initial spin angular momentum is converted into orbital angular momentum in analogy with the Einstein-de Haas effect. We investigate these conversion processes governed by the rotational viscous effect by analyzing the spacetime profiles of thermal vorticity and spin potential. Our PINNs-based framework provides the first numerical evidence for spin-orbit angular momentum conversion with fully nonlinear computational relativistic spin hydrodynamics.

papers.title: Odd-viscosity-induced instability in shear flows
papers.abstract: Odd viscosity is a nondissipative component of the viscosity tensor that arises in fluids with broken time-reversal symmetry. We show that, despite being energy-conserving, odd viscosity can qualitatively alter hydrodynamic stability by generating exponentially growing modes that are absent in conventional fluids. For plane Poiseuille flow, we derive the odd-viscous generalization of the Orr--Sommerfeld--Squire equations and find a new instability that first emerges for streamwise-uniform modes and extends to oblique modes. The instability exploits the non-normality of the linearized Navier--Stokes operator: conventional fluids support transiently growing disturbances through the lift-up mechanism, while odd viscosity closes a feedback loop between wall-normal velocity and vorticity, converting these disturbances into self-sustaining exponentially growing modes. This mechanism lowers the linear instability threshold by nearly two orders of magnitude, from $\mathrm{Re}_c \approx 5772$ to $\mathrm{Re}_c \approx 62$. More generally, we show that an energy-conserving coupling can destabilize a linearly stable system by sustaining the growth of otherwise transiently growing disturbances. Such a coupling thus triggers energy growth without directly supplying energy, by enabling continuous energy extraction from the background state. This establishes a mechanism for controlling stability in non-normal systems without direct energy dissipation or injection.

papers.title: Experimental Realization of Higher-order Topological Water Wave Crystal
papers.abstract: Free-surface water waves provide a macroscopic platform in which topological localization can be measured through surface-elevation fields. Higher-order topological phases offer a route to localizing wave modes at structural corners, yet their experimental realization in water-wave systems remains largely unexplored. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a water-wave higher-order topological crystal, where surface waves are confined to structural corners and spectrally identified through measured free-surface responses. Bulk band analysis and finite-system simulations predict topological edge and corner states in the designed structure, while frequency-resolved surface-elevation measurements confirm the corresponding localized modes. The measured spectra and field distributions reveal pronounced in-gap corner localization consistent with the predicted higher-order topological modes. These results establish surface water waves as a directly measurable platform for higher-order topological physics, enabling spatial localization and spectral characterization of hydrodynamic wave modes.

papers.title: An Enhanced Spectral Boundary Integral Method for Modeling Highly Nonlinear Water Waves in Variable Depth
papers.abstract: This paper presents a new numerical model based on the highly nonlinear potential flow theory for simulating the propagation of water waves in variable depth. A new set of equations for estimating the surface vertical velocity is derived based on the boundary integral equation considering the water depth variability. A successive approximation scheme is also proposed in this study for calculating the surface vertical velocity. With the usage of Fast Fourier Transform, the model can be efficiently used for simulating highly nonlinear water waves on large spatiotemporal scale in a phase-resolving approach. The new model is comprehensively verified and validated through simulating a variety of nonlinear wave phenomenon including free propagating solitary wave, wave transformations over submerged bar, Bragg reflection over undulating bars, nonlinear evolution of Peregrine breather, obliquely propagating uniform waves and extreme waves in crossing random seas. Good agreements are achieved between the numerical simulations and laboratory measurements, indicating that the new model is sufficiently accurate. A discussion is presented on the accuracy and efficiency of the present model, which is compared with the Higher-Order Spectral method. The results show that the present model can be significantly more efficient at the same level of accuracy. It is suggested that the new model developed in the paper can be reliably used to simulate the nonlinear evolution of ocean waves in phase-resolving approach to shed light on the dynamics of nonlinear wave phenomenon taking place on a large spatiotemporal scale, which may be computationally expensive by using other existing methods.

papers.title: Flame Bifurcation, Flashback Margins, and NOx Scaling in a Swirl-Stabilized Hydrogen Aero-Engine Combustor
papers.abstract: Burning neat hydrogen in aircraft turbines eliminates carbon emissions, yet rapid reaction rates trigger nozzle flashback hazards and high nitrogen oxide emissions across flight throttles. This study investigates aerothermal holding mechanisms, flashback safety margins, and emission pathways in a dual-swirl combustor across equivalence ratios from 0.55 to 1.00. Three-dimensional simulations combine curvature-corrected shear-stress transport turbulence closure, dual-rate finite-rate and eddy-dissipation chemical kinetics, and discrete ordinates radiation, validated against experimental laser benchmarks using ASME grid standards. Advancing engine throttle triggers a topological flame bifurcation from a faceplate-attached M-flame at lean idle to a lifted V-flame above equivalence ratio 0.895, while wall flashback safety indices consistently exceed 3.42. Nitric oxide emissions transition from water-chaperoned nitrous oxide intermediate reactions at lean idle (28.01 ppm, EINOx = 1.85 g/kg), scaling to 319.21 ppm (EINOx = 35.40 g/kg) at takeoff under thermal Zeldovich dominance, governed by a power-law exponent of 4.92. These findings deliver validated operability limits and establish an accessible workstation-based screening methodology for practical zero-carbon aero-engine combustor development.

papers.title: Active particle dynamics in uniform and patterned electroosmotic flows
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of self-propelled spheroidal particles in electroosmotic channel flows generated by uniform, patterned, and combined zeta-potential distributions. The coupling between self-propulsion, particle shape, and electroosmotic advection gives rise to distinct regimes of confinement and transport. For a uniform zeta potential, the dynamics reduce to a two-dimensional system in cross-stream position and orientation. We show that this system possesses a non-canonical Hamiltonian structure, allowing its phase-space organization to be characterized analytically. For spherical particles, the dynamics admit a nonlinear-pendulum description, yielding the characteristic oscillation frequency and extent of the confined region. The oscillation frequency depends non-monotonically on electrostatic screening and reaches a maximum at an intermediate Debye parameter. Spatially patterned zeta potentials reorganize the dynamics by generating counter-rotating vortices and coupling streamwise position, cross-stream position, and particle orientation. Numerical simulations and dynamical-systems analysis reveal regimes of single-cell confinement and cross-cell migration, controlled by particle shape and electrostatic screening. When uniform and patterned components coexist, mean electroosmotic advection competes with vortex-induced recirculation, producing transport sensitive to particle shape and initial conditions. Together, these results connect Hamiltonian phase-space dynamics in uniform electroosmotic flow to vortex-mediated trapping and transport in patterned flows, highlighting the potential of surface electrostatic patterning to control particle motion without altering channel geometry.

papers.title: Instability of streaky high-supersonic boundary layers over cooled walls
papers.abstract: We investigate the instability of streaks induced by free-stream vortical disturbances in cooled-wall high-supersonic boundary layers. Distinct types of instability modes are identified: modified Mack second modes, a newly discovered varicose secondary-instability mode and sinuous or varicose secondary-instability modes akin to those in incompressible boundary layers. Unique characteristics of the new secondary-instability mode are that its eigenfunctions concentrate in high-speed valley regions near the wall and feature intense temperature fluctuations at the wall. The streaks in high-supersonic boundary layers destabilise the three-dimensional secondary-instability modes, but suppress the growth of the modified Mack second modes, both radiating and non-radiating. The suppression of radiating modes amounts to a reduction of the two-dimensional noise they emit. Numerical results indicate that, unlike streaks in adiabatic-wall boundary layers, whose instability concentrates in low-speed peak regions away from the wall, the secondary instability of streaks in cooled-wall high-supersonic boundary layers occurs both in low-speed peak regions and in high-speed valley regions.

papers.title: Burning limits and the role of small scale turbulence in high Karlovitz number premixed flames
papers.abstract: Premixed flames exhibit a progressive enhancement in burning rates with turbulence, with the ultimate limits governed by the onset of local extinctions. Piloted premixed burners have enabled access to turbulence far exceeding the theoretically predicted extinction limits, with the measured flame speeds still improving. This study explores the role of small scale turbulence on the burning rates of premixed flames using a piloted high Karlovitz number burner. Premixed CH$_4$-air mixtures with equivalence ratios ($\phi$) from 0.7--1.0, stabilized using a $\phi$-matched pilot flame, were subjected to increasing rms fluctuating velocities, $u'$, up to 36.0 m/s. The experimental setup enables a progressive increase in turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) at smaller scales, with the Kolmogorov scales reaching approximately 4 $\mu$m under the highest turbulence condition. Global consumption flame speeds, $S_\mathrm{T,GC}$, derived from the binarized Planar Laser-Induced Fluorescence (PLIF) imaging of OH radicals, scale with turbulent diffusivity, $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{T}$. Further increases in $u'$, however, lead to a maximum and an eventual decline in flame speeds. The measured flame speeds exhibit a common scaling with the measured upstream $u'$. Assessments of the flame structure using CH-PLIF images further reveal progressive straining and extinction events with increasing $u'$ despite flames maintaining their flamelet-like appearance, suggesting that the observed limits derive from the increasing extinction propensity across the flame front. Finally, these findings are incorporated into a scaling relation accounting for the role of straining and extinctions in the observed flame-speed trends.

papers.title: Quantum HHL Algorithm for Solving 1D Linear Advection Equation Using Explicit and Implicit Finite Difference Schemes
papers.abstract: This study develops and implements a Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) quantum algorithm for solving a one-dimensional linear advection equation with periodic boundary conditions. The governing equation is first discretized using a classical finite difference (FD) scheme to obtain a linear system suitable for quantum solution. We present a newly designed, circuit-level implementation of HHL assembled from Qiskit circuit components and exploit the circulant structure of the periodic discretization matrices through Fourier-based matrix evolution. The HHL algorithm is benchmarked with three explicit schemes and one implicit scheme. The implicit scheme requires a nontrivial linear solve arising from the discretized PDE on progressively finer grids, whereas the explicit schemes provide different input fields for testing state preparation and reconstruction with identity coefficient matrices. HHL solution states are validated against direct classical solves in noiseless simulation. For hardware execution, the periodic matrix structure permits a Fourier implementation that applies reciprocal eigenvalues without phase estimation. Results on the IBM Rensselaer Nighthawk processor are compared at a shared final time. Noiseless reconstructed fields approach the transported profile on resolved grids, while substantial hardware errors remain for both explicit and implicit schemes. Crank-Nicolson remains exceptionally well-conditioned and utilizes similar circuit re sources to the explicit controls, proving that hardware degradation in our tests was not driven by poor matrix conditioning. Ultimately, this study shows new means for HHL algorithms to study quantum CFD problems involving advection equations with implicit time integrations, while demonstrating how state preparation and measurement affect the practical performance of quantum solvers on current devices.

papers.title: Optimizing synthetic jet placement for control stability in increasing Reynolds number flows based on deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: This study utilizes reinforcement learning algorithms to develop advanced control strategies for manipulating synthetic jets positioned on a cylinder, aiming to achieve effective flow control. It addresses critical challenges in achieving robust performance across moderate to high Reynolds numbers (Re) and varying jet placement configurations. The results demonstrate that placing synthetic jets near flow separation regions yields optimal control performance. At Re = 500, the multi-objective flow control strategy achieves up to 37.4% drag reduction and 99% suppression of lift oscillations, while completely suppressing vortex shedding. At Re = 1,000, drag reduction improves to 49.1%, with equally effective lift suppression and complete vortex shedding suppression. At Re = 2,000, the strategy achieves a maximum drag reduction of 58.8% and suppresses 90% of lift oscillations, although some residual wake instabilities persist. Additionally, synthetic jets effectively disrupted detached vortices and stabilized the wake, resulting in streamlined flow and suppressed vortex shedding. These findings underscore the pivotal influence of jet placement in optimizing flow control efficacy, while affirming the advanced capability of control strategies to tackle intricate challenges.

papers.title: Bistability in the stalling behavior of thick, cambered airfoils under elevated freestream turbulence
papers.abstract: The aerodynamic performance of a thick, cambered FFA-W3-301 airfoil section near and beyond stall was examined under elevated freestream turbulence using time-resolved surface pressure measurements for chord-based Reynolds numbers from 125,000 to 275,000. Three passive turbulence grids were used to isolate the effects of turbulence intensity and integral length scale, and the results were compared with a clean inflow. The elevated turbulence largely had a positive effect on the mean performance of the airfoil section, eliminating premature flow separation and recovering lift and drag polars more representative of a higher effective Reynolds number; however, resolving the lift in time showed that the time-averaged polars concealed bistable switching. The time-averaged lift was an occupancy-weighted average of two states, and conventional mean and standard-deviation statistics misrepresented the true post-stall unsteady loads. Beyond the maximum-lift angle of attack, the lift alternated repeatedly between two distinct levels with no characteristic frequency. At the highest tested Reynolds number, the switching persisted over an angle-of-attack range of up to nine degrees, more than an order of magnitude wider than that reported for a thin, symmetric section in a low turbulence inflow. The lift levels of the two states were also found to be nearly independent of the inflow turbulence level, whereas the fraction of time spent in each differed between turbulence conditions. conditionally averaged surface pressure distributions and proper orthogonal decomposition of the surface pressure consistently showed that neither state is fully attached; the states correspond to two positions of a single separation front on the suction side, a switching accurately captured by a single pressure mode from the decomposition.
